name: Lyonnais Francoprovençal, St. Martin-en-Haut
confidence_why: Kasstan 2015, the only first-hand phonetic description of this variety, shows stress falling unpredictably on the final or penultimate syllable (cela [səˈla] 'that' versus sela [ˈsøla] 'chair'), and Stich 2001 and Martin 1990 (as reported by Nagy 2000) agree that Francoprovençal stress is inherited from Latin and contrasts oxytones with paroxytones, the only variance being whether the right-edge window is two or three syllables.
catalog_citation: Kasstan, Jonathan Richard. 2015. Lyonnais (Francoprovençal). Journal of the International Phonetic Association 45(3) (Illustrations of the IPA). doi:10.1017/S0025100315000250
catalog_locator: p. 353, section 'Stress' (also p. 352-353 'Vowels' on preserved unstressed final vowels)
catalog_quote: Stress. Owing to the fact that Francoprovençal retains a number of Latin atonic vowels, the stress pattern can vary and can fall on either paroxytonic or oxytonic syllables (compare cela [səˈla] ‘that’ and sela [ˈsøla] ‘chair’). As with the Occitan varieties, this feature differentiates these Lyonnais varieties of Francoprovençal markedly from SF. ... Francoprovençal preserves a number of unstressed final vowels. For example, unstressed Latin atonic A is maintained as /a/, e.g. TABULAM > trâbla [ˈtʁɔbla] ‘table’, which also undergoes raising to [i] when preceded by a palatal, e.g. VACCAM > vache [ˈvaʃi] ‘cow’. ... Despite the variability in final vowels present in Francoprovençal, there is often a reduced vocalic quality in connected speech, and so schwa is also common in unstressed syllables.
sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title for fran1260: Nagy 2000 'Stress and schwa in Faetar' (Benjamins, CILT 212, pp. 238-254; Benjamins page could not be reached by automated download, Crossref shows no OA link). An open author's HTML version was found on Nagy's own site (ngn.artsci.utoronto.ca/zip/stress.schwa.zip), downloaded, unzipped and read in full; the reference was attached to fran1260 only by Glottolog's computerized assignment from the word 'faetar'), so relevance is another language or variety. Its finding (stress lexically marked, on the rightmost non-schwa vowel within the last three syllables, open or closed) and its second-hand statement on Gallic Francoprovençal (lexically marked within the last two syllables, minimal pair ['tsata] ~ [tsa'ta], Martin 1990:673) are consistent with the catalog's lexical coding for Lyonnais (Kasstan 2015) and with Stich 2001 already held by the project; nothing contradicts. It does not supersede Kasstan 2015, which describes the exact catalog variety. Nothing remains unread for this item; the Glottolog tagging error (Faetar -> fran1260 rather than faet1240) is worth noting in the per-language bibliography. Nagy's CV also lists 'Nagy 2000. Faetar. Munich: Lincom Europa (LW/M 299)', a descriptive grammar of Faetar (not open; abstract page saved), relevant only to faet1240.

new_statements.quote: Stress always appears on the rightmost non-schwa vowel of a word. The stressed syllable is always one of the last three syllables in the word. However, stress is not on a fixed syllable, counting from the left or from the right, nor is it consistently on either an odd or an even syllable. Furthermore, stress may be on either an open or closed syllable [...] Historical evidence also supports lexically marked stress, as Francoprovençal, the source language of Faetar, has lexically marked stress. Although Francoprovençal requires that stress be on one of the last two syllables, there are minimal pairs like ['†ata] 'sing, 2nd sg. imperative' vs. [†a'ta] 'sing, 2nd pl. imperative' (Martin 1990:673).

new_statements.quote: Briefly, it is also worth mentioning the stress pattern of Francoprovençal. We saw above that Francoprovençal can be contrasted with SF, which is rigidly an oxytonic language. However, given that Francoprovençal retains a number of Latin atonic vowels word-finally, like Occitan, it is a paroxytonic language, where stress can either fall on the antepenultimate, penultimate, or final syllable (e.g. for example ‘cela’ (‘that’) [səˈla], and ‘chaise’ (‘chair’) [ˈsøla]). [p. 48] || In short, given the distinct lack of unstressed final vowels in either the northern oïl varieties, or SF, the syllable stress pattern in French is distinctively oxytonic. However, in Francoprovençal the stress can be either paroxytonic or proparoxytonic. [p. 30]

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the existing lexical/right-edge-window reading (Nagy 2000 on Faetar: last three syllables; Martin 1990 via Nagy: last two syllables). Kasstan states the window for Francoprovençal generally as antepenult/penult/final (three syllables), i.e. the wider of the two windows, and adds a sociolinguistic caveat: paroxytonic stress is reported to be levelling toward final stress in northern varieties in contact with French. The statement is about Francoprovençal as a whole, but the thesis's French fieldwork sites are les monts du Lyonnais including Saint-Martin-en-Haut (p. 122), so it is closer to the catalog variety than the Faetar-based existing statement. It does not contradict th…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Francoprovençal (as a whole, not a single village variety) is a 'paroxytonic' language in the Romance sense: unlike French, it keeps unstressed word-final vowels, so word stress is not fixed on the final syllable but falls on the antepenultimate, penultimate or final syllable depending on the word (a three-syllable right-edge window; p. 30 gives it as paroxytonic or proparoxytonic). The thesis gives no rule for choosing among these positions, so placement is lexically determined within the window.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 30 reports Costa and Bert (2014: 195) as arguing that paroxytonic stress is being levelled out (toward French-style final stress) in northern Francoprovençal varieties in contact with oïl French. No village-specific stress data; the phonology overview (sec. 2.6) is explicitly 'adapted from Stich (1998); Nagy (2000); Martin (2005; 2006); Tuaillon (2007) and most recently Kasstan (2015)' (p. 44), so the stress statement is a synthesis of the descriptive literature rather than a first-hand measurement.
new_statements.identity_note: Kasstan 2015 describes Francoprovençal generically in its stress statements (sec. 2.5-2.6, an overview adapted from Stich 1998, Nagy 2000, Martin 2005/2006, Tuaillon 2007); it does not give stress data for Saint-Martin-en-Haut specifically, although Saint-Martin-en-Haut, Rontalon, Saint-Symphorien-sur-Coise and Yzeron in les monts du Lyonnais are its French fieldwork sites (p. 122), alongside the Canton of Valais in Switzerland. The existing catalog statement is first-hand for Faetar (faet1240, a sister language in southern Italy) and only second-hand for Francoprovençal proper.

readall_conflicts: No real disagreement. Kasstan 2015 gives the window as antepenultimate/penultimate/final (p. 48) and, more loosely, 'paroxytonic or proparoxytonic' (p. 30), whereas the existing statement drawn from Nagy 2000 gives a three-syllable window for Faetar and a two-syllable window (via Martin 1990: 673) for Francoprovençal; Stich 2001 (already held by the project, pp. 225-227) also gives one of the last two syllables. The three-way choice in Kasstan p. 48 includes final stress, which the p. 30 sentence omits; this is an internal looseness in a synthetic overview, not a claim about a different stress type. All sources agree that stress is not fixed and sits within a right-edge window of two or three syllables; the only substantive addition is the reported levelling of paroxytones toward final stress in northern varieties in contact with French (Costa and Bert 2014: 195, as cited by Kasstan p. 30).

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: every segment of the deciding quotation is verbatim in the Cambridge Core PDF we hold of Kasstan 2015 at p. 353 'Stress' (and p. 352-353 'Vowels'), locator correct; only cosmetic issues (segment order, added period after heading). (2) Deciding source: a 2015 JIPA Illustration of the exact variety, i.e. a peer-reviewed phonetic description, not pedagogical or second-hand; the near-minimal pair cela [səˈla] vs sela [ˈsøla] (both CV.CV, both final [a]) justifies lexical within a right-edge two-syllable window rather than a weight/final-vowel rule. (3) Independent confirmation downloaded now: Stich 2001 (Paris V thesis, open) states for Francoprovençal generally that stress falls on one of the last two syllables and that the oxytone/paroxytone opposition is phonemic (tsantâ 'chanter' ~ tsanta 'chante!'), matching our classification; its caveat that north-western 'francoprovençal dégradé'

tone.quote: Finally, as far as word-level prosody is concerned, FP retains from Latin a number of final monophthongs /i e a o ɔ ɔ̃/ which can carry grammatical functions (e.g. case morphology) or phonemic distinctions, and which tend not to carry stress. Accordingly, the stress pattern in FP can vary, and can fall on either penultimate or final syllables. As final vowels are often unstressed, there is in practice significant variation in their realisation, and in some regions, the vowel sounds /e/ and /o ɔ/ in particular are argued to be undergoing some merger (Stich 1998: 65).
tone.locator: p. 894, sec. 1.2 (general phonology of Francoprovençal), paragraph before 1.2.1 'Nendaz Francoprovençal'
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.summary: No tone; word stress penultimate or final (lexical, tied to retained final atonic vowels).

sources.citation: Roullet, Stefania. 1999. Accent et intonation dans le parler de deux villages valdôtains - Sarre et Cogne. Géolinguistique 8: 197-235. doi:10.3406/geol.1999.1137

tone.quote: -la fréquence fondamentale est le paramètre le plus important dans la réalisation de l’accent, à Sarre comme à Cogne ; ... Sur la base de cette étude, il serait en tout cas incorrecte d’affirmer que l’accent francoprovençal est de type intensif, l’intensité étant, sans l’ombre d’un doute, le paramètre le moins concerné par l’accent. En revanche, on peut définir sans crainte l’accent réalisé dans la variété de Sarre comme accent tonal ou, si l’on préfère pitch accent, la même définition pouvant être employée également pour celui de Cogne, mais avec plus de prudence, vue l’importance considérable du paramètre durée dans la réalisation de ce dernier.
tone.locator: pp. 203-204, sec. 3.1.1 'Les paramètres fréquence fondamentale, durée et intensité dans les différents types d'accent' (closing paragraph of 3.1 before 3.2 'L'intonation')
tone.translation: -fundamental frequency is the most important parameter in the realisation of the accent, at Sarre as at Cogne; ... On the basis of this study it would in any case be incorrect to claim that the Francoprovençal accent is of the intensity type, intensity being without any doubt the parameter least involved in the accent. On the other hand, the accent realised in the Sarre variety can safely be defined as a tonal accent or, if one prefers, pitch accent; the same definition can also be used for that of Cogne, but with more caution, given the considerable importance of the duration parameter in its realisation.
tone.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone.summary: No lexical tone; culminative word stress (oxytone/paroxytone) realised mainly by F0, duration secondary (Cogne), intensity least.

sources.citation: Tuaillon, Gaston. 1988. Néo-oxytons en francoprovençal grenoblois : datation du phénomène. Géolinguistique 4: 93-116. doi:10.3406/geol.1988.1081

tone.quote: Les patois francoprovençaux peuvent, dans certains contextes phonétiques, déplacer l'accent étymologique du mot. Duraffour a étudié ces phénomènes dans le chapitre I ("L'intensité : ses variations et ses effets") des Phénomènes généraux d'évolution phonétique dans les dialectes franco-provençaux (Grenoble, 1932). ... d) le transport d'accent sur la finale atone. La présente étude ne s'occupera que du dernier cas.
tone.translation: The Francoprovençal patois can, in certain phonetic contexts, displace the etymological accent of the word. Duraffour studied these phenomena in chapter I ('Intensity: its variations and its effects') of the Phénomènes généraux d'évolution phonétique dans les dialectes franco-provençaux (Grenoble, 1932). ... d) the transfer of the accent onto the unstressed final syllable. The present study deals only with the last case.
tone.summary: No tone; lexical stress with dialectal stress shift onto final atonic vowels (neo-oxytones).

sources.citation: Mercadal, Roland. 1977. Les néo-oxytons en francoprovençal : tentative d'explication. Revue de linguistique romane 41: 114-119. doi:10.5169/seals-399641 (e-periodica:https://www.e-periodica.ch/digbib/view?pid=rlr-001:1977:41::124)

tone.quote: J'ai recueilli mes informations dans un hameau de la Commune de Laval, située dans la chaîne de Belledonne (Isère). Cette Commune s'inscrit dans la zone grenobloise où sont créées les formes oxytoniques nouvelles. J'y ai relevé 80 néo-oxytons, qui constituent la base de ma réflexion. [...] Ce qui m'amène à la conclusion suivante : l'importance donnée à la finale dans la longueur — sans que le timbre soit modifié — aurait concurrencé et desservi la voyelle de la syllabe pénultième tonique, dont le timbre se serait peu à peu fermé et affaibli, au point de devenir parfois complètement neutre ; ne pouvant garder sa place, l'accent se serait déporté sur la finale.
tone.locator: p. 114 (sec. I) and p. 118 (conclusion of sec. II); summary p. 118-119
tone.translation: I collected my information in a hamlet of the Commune of Laval, in the Belledonne range (Isère). This Commune lies in the Grenoble zone where the new oxytonic forms are created. I recorded 80 neo-oxytones there, which form the basis of my reflection. [...] Which brings me to the following conclusion: the importance given to the final in length -- without the timbre being modified -- would have competed with and weakened the vowel of the stressed penultimate syllable, whose timbre would gradually have closed and weakened, sometimes becoming completely neutral; unable to keep its place, the accent would have moved onto the final.
tone.summary: No tone content. The article is about word stress: in the Laval (Belledonne, Isère) Francoprovençal dialect 80 singular nouns/adjectives (90% feminines in -a/-e) have shifted stress from the penult to the final atonic vowel (neo-oxytones); Mercadal argues the shift was caused by weakening/closing of the penultimate vowel, itself caused by a local tendency to lengthen final vowels; morphological s…

tone.quote: L'accent d'intensité conforme en général, à Vaux et en franco-provençal, à l'état de l'ensemble des langues romanes. Il a subi cependant des déplacements caractéristiques du groupement linguistique [...] l'accent de la première syllabe est surtout un accent de hauteur, la deuxième gardant son intensité plus grande. [...] nous nous servons de termes (« accentuée, préaccentuée, postaccentuée » d'une part — « intonée » de l'autre) qui ne peuvent prêter à aucune confusion entre l'accent d'intensité, ou accent proprement dit, « accent » tout court, et l'accent de hauteur ou «ton ».
tone.locator: ch. I 'L'intensité: ses variations et ses effets', p. 1 (Sommaire); p. 10; p. 17 n. 1 (lines for article pp. 1); also p. 4 on durations and pitch intervals under intensity
tone.translation: The intensity (stress) accent conforms in general, at Vaux and in Franco-Provencal, to the state of the Romance languages as a whole. It has however undergone displacements characteristic of the linguistic grouping [...] the accent of the first syllable is above all a pitch accent, the second keeping its greater intensity. [...] we use terms ('accented, pre-accented, post-accented' on the one hand -- 'intoned' on the other) which cannot lead to any confusion between the intensity accent, or accent proper, 'accent' for short, and the pitch accent or 'tone'.
tone.summary: No lexical tone. Duraffour describes the prosody of Vaux (Bugey) and Francoprovençal generally as a very strong intensity (stress) accent in the ordinary Romance position, with FP-specific displacements (hiatus -> final; recent paroxytonic tendency; retraction onto a long initial; transfer onto atonic final -a).
